headlines.article_text: Musk: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas next year Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Elon Musk said Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas around mid-2027. Musk said the change will make room for increased production of Tesla’s Cybercab robotaxi. The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales and has faced several recalls. In this article TSLA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A Tesla Cybertruck at the company's store in Colma, California, US, on Monday, April 21, 2025. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Friday said the electric vehicle maker will "be winding down" production of the Cybertruck at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year. Musk , who hailed the Cybertruck as the future of the pickup truck segment , said in a post on X early Friday morning that the end of production at the massive facility would make room for manufacturing of its Cybercab robotaxi. The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company's plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward. Musk did not say whether the company would produce the Cybertruck at a different facility, but he later responded to a user on X who called the update an "end of an era" and said the Cybertruck was the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made." "True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time," Musk said. Tesla began Cybertruck deliveries in late 2023 . The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. watch now VIDEO 12:23 12:23 Why Cybertruck sales have struggled Autos The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk's pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000. "Trucks have been the same for a very long time," Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019. "Like 100 years. Trucks have been basically the same. We want to try something different." While Tesla does not break out its sales by model or region, Cox Automotive estimated sales of the Cybertruck last year at 20,237 units in the U.S., down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. One big buyer of the Cybertruck last year was Musk's aerospace and tech conglomerate, SpaceX , which spent $131 million buying up the angular steel trucks at Tesla's suggested retail price, according to a SpaceX financial filing . The distinct look of the vehicle made some owners a target of rude gestures and more serious road rage, one owner told CNBC last May , after Musk became the biggest funder of Donald Trump 's presidential campaign and led the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, an effort to slash the federal workforce and regulations. Wired wrote in an October 2025 feature story, "There is likely no object that feels more emblematic of US president Donald Trump's return to the White House than the Tesla Cybertruck ." The magazine interviewed owners who described being spit on and sworn at due to their choice of vehicle. The Cybertruck's specifications also fell short of those Tesla advertised early on, and in some cases fell short of those offered by leading fuel-burning pickups. There have also been many quality and production problems associated with the vehicles. The 2024 Tesla Cybertruck was the subject of 11 voluntary recalls, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration website. Issues ranged from a "trapped" acceleration pedal risk that could cause unintended acceleration, to software defects and an inverter fault that could result in sudden loss of drive power. headlines.article_text: Nasdaq drops into correction territory — here’s what typically happens next Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article .IXIC NDAQ Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Nasdaq 100 signage at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images The Nasdaq Composite plunged into correction territory on Thursday. History shows more selling can follow in the near term, but a recovery eventually takes hold three months later. The tech-heavy index slid more than 5% on Thursday, closing more than 11% below its record reached last month. On Wall Street, any decline greater than 10% is a correction. A 20% pullback qualifies as a bear market. Across 10 previous correction episodes over the last decade, selloffs in 2025, 2022, 2020 and 2018 were followed by further rough selling over the next one month. But the Nasdaq was back to rally mode again after six months for all those occasions except one: 2022. Overall, the Nasdaq gained an average of 9.41% from the correction bottom over the following three months and 17.03% over six months. The January 2022 correction was the one that offered a harsher outcome. The Nasdaq lost another 18.3% over the next six months and was down 24.3% a year later. Nasdaq Composite Deena Zaidi and Nick Wells The catalyst for this correction was Democrats sweeping the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. The party also made significant gains in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor after campaigning on an immediate moratorium for data center development. Investors are now weighing whether tighter state-level restrictions could slow data center construction, putting pressure on companies tied to the artificial intelligence trade. Frank Cappelleri, founder of CappThesis, pointed to past midterm election cycles for guidance and found that points to more volatility in the near term as well. The chart analyst said the Nasdaq was higher 12 months after the election in all but one of 13 midterm cycles since 1974. "The caveat is that the path can be a volatile one," he said. Cappelleri pointed to 2018, when the Nasdaq rallied the day after Democrats won the House. A sharp December sell-off followed, but the index was ultimately about 15% higher a year after the election, he said.
